chunks.text: --- tags: [books, canon, 4P, influence, framework, leadership] type: canonical-document status: v0.1 — draft (target lock: June 2026) created: 2026-06-21 --- # Influence System Canon The living document governing [[Chris Binion]]'s entire influence framework and publishing body of work. All books, masterclasses, LinkedIn posts, and enterprise programs must trace back to this document. **Canon lock target:** June 2026 (v1.0). After lock, changes are deliberate and rare. --- ## The Core Claim Influence is not a positional attribute. It is an emergent system. Sustained influence arises from the interaction of four factors — Purpose, Passion, Performance, and People — not from authority, charisma, or control. It is cultivated through alignment, consistency, and relational credibility over time. It is measurable and observable as an outcome, not a personality trait. --- ## The 4P Model ### Purpose (P1) **Definition:** The clarity of why you do what you do. Purpose is not a slogan or mission statement. It is the operating conviction that shapes decisions when clarity is absent and pressure is present. **What it is:** - The anchor that creates coherence across decisions - The reason someone endures sustained tension without losing direction - What makes consistency legible to others **What it is NOT:** - A vision statement - Motivation in the conventional sense ("I feel inspired") - Something derived from personality or passion alone **Failure mode:** Purpose stated but not operational — it doesn't appear in actual choices, only in presentations. --- ### Passion (P2) **Definition:** The sustained energy and ownership someone brings to the work over time. Not excitement or enthusiasm. The willingness to care about quality when no one is watching. **What it is:** - Investment that doesn't require external reward to persist - The thing that makes someone's work distinctly theirs - The difference between compliance and contribution **What it is NOT:** - Emotional intensity or charisma - Enthusiasm for novelty - The desire to be seen caring **Failure mode:** Passion misread as personality type — introversion or calm appearance confused with absence of passion. --- ### Performance (P3) **Definition:** The visible, consistent delivery of results that others can rely on. Performance establishes credibility. Without it, purpose and passion are theoretical. **What it is:** - Reliability that compounds over time - The evidence others use to trust your judgment - What converts good intentions into influence **What it is NOT:** - Achievement at any cost - Raw output disconnected from values - Optimization at the expense of people or sustainability **Failure mode:** Performance without purpose becomes a reputation for results without trust. Others comply but don't commit. --- ### People (P4) **Definition:** The relational dimension of influence — how someone treats, develops, and accounts for the people involved in or affected by their work. **What it is:** - The transmission layer of influence: your ideas spread through people, not past them - The test of whether influence is generative or extractive - How leaders multiply impact beyond their direct contribution **What it is NOT:** - Being liked - Avoiding conflict - Relationship-building as a political strategy **Failure mode:** People treated as resources rather than participants. Influence expands short-term and collapses when key people leave. --- ## Interaction Rules (P × P) The 4Ps do not operate independently.

Others carry your language and extend your reach. | --- ## Failure Modes (System-Level) 1. **Single-P dominance** — treating one P as sufficient (e.g., "my performance speaks for itself") 2. **Isolation error** — applying the model to one person without accounting for system dynamics 3. **Episodic application** — using the framework only in high-stakes moments, not as a consistent operating lens 4. **Vocabulary without practice** — speaking the language of 4P without it changing actual decisions 5. **Influence as outcome, not process** — measuring results instead of the system that produces them --- ## Misapplication Warnings - **Do not use 4P as a personality typing system.** It does not classify people — it describes behaviors and system conditions. - **Do not treat the Ps as a hierarchy.** No P outranks another. All four must be present and interacting. - **Do not teach Passion as enthusiasm.** The misread causes people to conclude they don't have it. - **Do not reduce People to "likability."** Influence through people requires accountability, not just warmth. - **Do not use this framework for self-promotion.** Influence described outward ("I have influence") signals its absence. --- ## Teaching Guardrails **Facilitators must:** - Know the definitions before teaching the applications - Use examples from the canon books, not improvised analogies - Correct any Ps-as-personality misread immediately - Always situate the framework as systemic, not individual **Facilitators must NEVER improvise:** - Alternate definitions of any P - New interaction rules not in the canon - Applications in domains not yet covered by a canon book - Claims about what the model predicts --- ## Scope Boundaries **Signal to Action covers:** The gap between awareness and action — why people hesitate even when they know what's right. **Influence covers:** The 4P model as a conceptual system — what it is and why it matters. **Foundations of Influence covers:** How to teach and apply the 4P model at scale — definitions, visuals, onboarding.

Frames ChatGPT as a cognitive companion — not a shortcut or creative replacement — that translates summary-oriented, action-driven thinking into coherent prose without diluting judgment, intent, or authorship. Explores the friction many capable thinkers experience when their minds move naturally toward synthesis and decision rather than description and narrative. Shows how conversational AI can serve as scaffolding that enables expansion, organization, and refinement of thought. chunks.text: --- tags: [faith, theology, doctrine, baptism, salvation] type: doctrinal-reference source: Blog posts — academic papers from M.A. Religious Studies, Liberty University (2012) created: 2026-06-21 --- # Doctrinal Positions Chris Binion's theological convictions, derived from his own academic writing, pastoral experience, and personal faith. These are not casual opinions — they are argued, researched, and deeply held. --- ## Law and Grace **Position: The Law is an expression of God's love, not a condition for relationship.** From his analysis of Exodus 20:2 — "I am the LORD your God" — God declared relationship *before* giving any commandments. The Commandments were given *because* of relationship, not as conditions *for* it. This means: - Works-based salvation is not just theologically wrong — it is fundamentally unstable. It leaves the person always unsure of their standing, never certain, always striving. - "If salvation were based on works, how good is good enough? Does God keep score?" — He finds the logical incoherence of works-based systems as damning as the scriptural case against them. - Keeping the Law is an expression of gratitude and love toward God — not a transaction to earn favor. - God's grace "completely gets rid of the flawed works-based system and makes it freely available to everyone." This same logic appears in his Romans paper and his baptism paper — consistent across all his theological writing. ## Faith and Reason (Christology) **Position: Faith and reason are not in opposition — they provide context for each other.** From his survey of three Christological approaches: - **Christology from Above:** Trusts Scripture without requiring historical proof; Christ known through the church and Word - **Christology from Below:** Requires rational proof; applies standard historical methods to Christ's claims - **Erickson's Alternative (Chris's position):** Revelation is both historical events and their interpretation; faith provides the starting point for reason; reason operates within the context of faith to understand what it otherwise could not > "Faith provides the perspective or starting point from which reason may function, enabling one to understand what otherwise could not be understood." He is neither fideist (faith alone, reason irrelevant) nor rationalist (reason must independently verify faith). He holds them in active synthesis. This is consistent with how he writes — always marshaling both Scripture and evidence, never treating them as competitors. ## Salvation **Position: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ alone.** - Basis: Romans 3:21-26, Romans 10:9-13, John 3:16 - Faith in Christ — not works, not sacraments, not ritual — is the sole basis for salvation - The Holy Spirit regenerates the believer upon confession and faith - Righteousness is imputed to the new believer by Christ; it is received, not earned > "Paul never mentions baptism as an essential ingredient to his comprehensive argument for salvation. Surely, something that is essential for salvation would be mentioned within these verses." — Chris Binion --- ## Baptism **Position: Believer's Baptism (Baptist view)** Baptism does not regenerate — it testifies to regeneration that has already occurred.

Deathbed confessions, people who believe before they can be baptized — these are saved. A theology requiring baptism for salvation places something other than Christ's finished work at the center of salvation, which contradicts Scripture. **Historical position:** Consistent with the Baptist Faith and Message (Southern Baptist) and the Baptist Confession of Faith of 1646. **Historical survey Chris traced:** - Early church → tied baptism and Holy Spirit closely but still prioritized faith (Philip and the Ethiopian, Acts 8) - Tertullian → hardened baptism into a law, first to say "without baptism, salvation is attainable by none" - Augustine → softened this; confession of Christ has same efficacy as baptism for the dying - Luther and Calvin → both taught baptismal regeneration, but tied it to faith - Anabaptists → rejected infant baptism; required public confession before baptism - Baptist tradition → codified believer's baptism; baptism follows and testifies to salvation **Chris's conclusion:** Baptism developed over time as a theology distorted from its original Scripture purpose. The New Testament pattern is belief followed by baptism, not baptism producing belief. --- ## The Holy Spirit - The Holy Spirit indwells believers at conversion - Speaking in tongues and other manifestations are evidences of the Spirit's work (Acts 10 — Cornelius's household received the Spirit, evidenced outwardly, before water baptism) - Chris's background is Southern Baptist / Pentecostal Evangelical — he holds both the Baptist doctrinal precision and openness to the Spirit's active work --- ## The Church - The church is the body of Christ, headed by Jesus Christ - Members are those who have trusted Christ's finished work by faith - Purpose: to glorify God by loving him and making him known to the lost world - Church planting as expression of this — Chris has planted two churches himself --- ## Scripture - The entire Bible is the inspired Word of God, written by men moved by the Holy Spirit - Scripture is without error - Authoritative and sufficient — "I believe the entire Bible is the inspired Word of God" --- ## Church Governance **Position: Modified Presbyterian model — elder plurality, pastor as "first among equals"** He rejects both extremes from firsthand experience: - **Pure congregational model** — power drifts to family patriarchs/matriarchs ("Grandma Hunter"), not the called pastor. Small group events draw ~80%. That's an 800% effectiveness increase. - All small group leadership in pairs — each pair must recruit and train a second pair → multiplication built into the structure - Church-wide outreach events were explicitly NOT part of the LifePoint strategy **Discipleship defined four ways (Matthew 4:18-20):** 1. Made Jesus Lord of life 2. In a process of relational discipleship with maturing Christians 3. Becoming Christ-like 4. Committed to the mission of Christ **Acts 1 before Acts 2:** Before seeking an Acts 2 experience (movement, growth, power), the team must first go through Acts 1 preparation — removing self-centeredness, over-confidence, division, insecurity, hypocrisy, and confusion. Then: prayer, mission review, team building, witness preparation, and welcoming the Holy Spirit. This model is not theoretical for Chris — he implemented it at LifePoint and wrote about it actively while planting. ## Sexual Abuse and the Church **Position: The church has a two-fold responsibility — prevention and healing.** Written August 2012 — his most pastoral blog post, directly applicable to his Scouting and youth ministry work. **The argument:** 1. Sexual sin is uniquely personal and destructive (1 Cor. 6:18 — "sins against his own body") 2. Victims often have their sense of identity and worth damaged; the church must understand this 3. The church must be proactive: policies, protocols, boundaries, AND healing programs 4. Silence in the pulpit on sexual sin propagates mystery and stigma — pastors must have courage to speak where the Bible speaks 5. Prevention is an act of love; healing is a command of Christ **Practical implications he named:** - Education on God's design for sex within marriage - Education on healing available in Christ - Safe, honest spaces for victims to share and receive acceptance and accountability - Church acceptance — the congregation must be prepared to receive people who are hurting **Connection to Scouting:** This theology directly informs his mandatory reporting stance and Youth Protection emphasis in [[Missions/Troop 95]]. chunks.text: He has been thinking about this responsibility since at least 2012. ## Covenant Theology **Position: Scripture is a unified covenant history culminating in Christ.** From a September 2011 academic review of Christopher J.H. Wright's *Knowing Jesus through the Old Testament* (written while serving as chaplain in Baghdad). The five major covenants form a cumulative structure, each building on the last: | Covenant | Scope | Core Promise | |----------|-------|-------------| | Noahic | All humanity | God preserves life; never destroys by flood again | | Abrahamic | All nations through Israel | Posterity, special relationship with God, land; all nations blessed through Abraham's seed | | Mosaic | Israel | Delivered from Egypt; exclusive loyalty to Yahweh expected | | Davidic | House of David | Eternal kingship; a model of how to follow God | | New (Jeremiah 31) | All nations | New relationship, new obedience, law written on hearts, universal knowledge of God | All five are fulfilled in Christ — not symbolically, but structurally. He completes what each covenant promised. **Key insight that moved Chris personally:** > "I have never thought of Christ as being the personification of Israel, nor Israel being a typology for Christ." He was genuinely surprised by the typological identification: Christ as "Son of God" in the same sense Israel was "God's firstborn son" — the same Father/son language applied to both. Christ doesn't just come *from* Israel; he is the individual fulfillment of what Israel as a collective was always meant to be. **On covenants and human response:** Wright's principle Chris engaged: "They call for human response, but they are not based on it, nor motivated by it." The covenants are God's initiative and God's guarantee — the required response is real but doesn't condition the promise. This is structurally consistent with his law/grace position (see above). ## Kingdom Theology **Position: The Kingdom of God has both personal and social/ethical dimensions.** > "Wherever God reigns and where He reigns, compassion and justice must reign too." This isn't a strong social gospel position — his soteriology is clearly personal and substitutionary. But he holds that the Kingdom is not only spiritual. The ethics of the Kingdom (care for the poor, justice, compassion) are natural expressions of God's reign in a community. This shows up in his missions approach: the three rules at Crossroads, the feeding program at LifePoint, the unchurched ministry posture. ## What These Positions Mean for Monday Chris is not a casual or cultural Christian. He has: - Studied historical theology through patristic sources (Tertullian, Justin Martyr, Augustine, Calvin, Luther) - Written academic defenses of Baptist soteriology - Applied Scripture to doctrine carefully, not emotionally - Planted churches and baptized believers under these convictions When faith topics arise, Monday should engage at this level of depth — not with surface spiritual platitudes. He wants theological substance, not encouragement language. --- ## Related Notes [[Knowledge/Faith Journey]] · [[Faith/Ministry History]] · [[Faith/Faith Action Plan]] · [[Faith/Church]] · [[Books/The Mystery of the Name]] · [[Books/The Apprenticeship of Jesus]] · [[Chris Binion]]

chunks.text: --- tags: [faith, church-planting, strategy, historical, LifePoint] type: historical-reference source: LifePoint Church Strategic Plan.docx (2013, written by Chris Binion) status: historical — Chris does not pursue church planting now created: 2026-06-21 --- # LifePoint Church Strategic Plan (2013) A full strategic plan for LifePoint Church, Alexandria, KY — written entirely by [[Chris Binion]] before the church launched. He describes it as "100% by me...these taught me much of what I know today" but notes it is historical: he does not pursue church planting now. **Status:** The church launched August 2013 and closed Spring 2014. The plan represents his thinking at the time, not a current pursuit. --- ## Why This Document Matters Chris wrote a McKinsey-quality strategic plan for a church plant at the same time he was starting a QC Manager role at Thermo Fisher (February 2013). Demographic studies, competitive model analysis, 5-phase discipleship pipeline, replication model, goals with measurable outcomes — the same systems-level thinking that later drove $20M+ in Thermo Fisher impact and the 4P publishing framework was already fully formed here. This document is the earliest full expression of how Chris thinks when given a problem and a blank page. --- ## The Foundation **Mission:** LifePoint exists to lead people into a growing relationship with Jesus Christ. **Vision:** Create a church un-churched people love to attend. **Core Values:** 1. **Biblical Authority** — God's Word is ultimate truth; 2 Tim 3:16-17 2. **Relationship** — intimacy with God linked with how we treat each other 3. **Community** — personally investing in the lives of others; Heb 10:24-25 4. **Relational Evangelism** — Christianity is contagious; share through relationship 5. **Service** — time, talent, and treasure for God by serving others 6. **Discipleship** — disciples make disciples 7. **Humility** — gratitude and dependence on God for everything --- ## Why Alexandria Chris did a formal market analysis: - Campbell County is the **10th most un-churched county in Kentucky** - **93% of the population is un-churched** - **164,071 people** within 10 miles of Alexandria won't attend church this week - The Barna Group found that in Northern Kentucky: 32% are un-churched, 81% are de-churched (used to attend, stopped) - Younger generations are moving further from God with each generation He also studied demographics in 5/10/15-mile rings: average age 35, predominantly married middle-class families, educated, college degrees, financially stable. The Barna data showed this region prefers teaching, serving the needy, and inquirer-friendly environments over evangelism-focused churches. --- ## The Model: Foyer → Living Room → Kitchen Adapted from Andy Stanley's North Point Community Church: | Environment | Purpose | Analogous to | |-------------|---------|--------------| | **Foyer** | Open, welcoming, safe for guests | Entry event / bridge activity | | **Living Room** | Connecting, relationship-building | Interest group / secondary event | | **Kitchen** | Small group — where life happens | LifeGroup / deep community | All roads at LifePoint led to small groups. Every ministry pointed inward to the Kitchen.

chunks.text: --- tags: [faith, ministry, pastoral, history, calling] type: ministry-history source: Binion Ministry Resume.doc created: 2026-06-21 --- # Ministry History [[Chris Binion]]'s pastoral and ministry record. This ran largely in parallel with his professional science career — not as a separate chapter, but as a simultaneous calling that was expressed at every stage. He has served as a church planter, pastor, associate pastor, youth minister, missionary, and military base chaplain (informal). The thread throughout is evangelism, discipleship, and building community from scratch. --- ## Pastoral Timeline ### Immanuel United Methodist Church — Lakeside Park, KY **Sunday Night Live Missions Coordinator** *September 2014 – [Current as of ministry resume]* Oversees outreach ministry at the 5th and Greenup facility. Furthers Immanuel's mission to make disciples of Jesus Christ for the transformation of the world through sharing faith and serving others. --- ### LifePoint Church — Alexandria, KY **Pastor / Church Planter** *August 2013 – April 2014* Started a new church in Alexandria, KY. Led team in evangelistic outreach and feeding program. Connected multiple ministries for mission work in Covington. Served as clergy on South-east Emmaus walks. Church closed Spring 2014. *Note: This was during the same period Chris joined Thermo Fisher (Feb 2013). The transition from chemistry to corporate began while he was simultaneously planting a church.* **The LifePoint Model (documented in Chris's own writing):** Chris implemented a sophisticated organizational system at LifePoint: - Small group as the heart of all church ministry — not a supplement to Sunday service - All small group leadership in pairs; each pair required to recruit and train a second pair - 101 (basics, required for all members) and 201 (leadership development) training classes - Church-wide outreach deliberately excluded — replaced entirely by small group outreach events - **80/10 rule:** Church-wide events draw ~10% participation; small group events draw ~80% → 800% effectiveness multiplier He applied the same organizational leverage logic here that he later applied to Thermo Fisher immersive programs and the 4P framework. The multiplication model (leaders who make leaders), the pair structure, the small group as the scalable unit — these are all systems-level thinking about organizational effectiveness, not just pastoral intuition. The church closed Spring 2014, but the model was sound. This is a chapter where the mission was right and the conditions didn't hold. --- ### Living Water — Alexandria, KY **Pastor** *February 2013 – August 2013* Worked to revitalize a struggling church plant. Reorganization, vision-casting, started outreach and missions programs. --- ### JSS Shield — Baghdad, Iraq **Pastor (informal chaplain)** *November 2010 – October 2011* This was a powerful and defining chapter. Assumed responsibility for spiritual growth, evangelism, and pastoral care for a military base in Baghdad that had no chaplain — while working professionally as a forensic chemist with DynCorp International. > "Experienced a powerful move of God by overseeing ministries in which over 100 people came to know Christ and followed him in baptism in an Islamic country." Started a successful multicultural small group ministry and men's and women's ministry. Equipped a Sierra Leone and Ugandan pastor in church planting in their respective countries; mentoring continued via Skype.

chunks.text: --- tags: [leadership, values, philosophy, identity] type: knowledge-note created: 2026-06-21 --- # Leadership Philosophy [[Chris Binion]] is a builder-leader. He does not lead from position — he leads from vision, mission clarity, and high standards. ## Builder-Leader Characteristics - **Mission clarity** — knows why the team exists before managing how - **High standards** — mediocrity is not acceptable; neither is the appearance of progress without it - **Honesty** — tells the truth, including uncomfortable truths - **Strategic imagination** — thinks ahead; sees what isn't yet - **Execution** — strategy without execution is fantasy - **Autonomy with accountability** — trusts people and holds them to results - **People development** — leadership multiplies through people, not despite them - **Practical excellence** — quality in the actual output, not just the vision ## What Frustrates Him in Leadership - Bureaucracy that protects process at the expense of outcome - Mediocrity tolerated in the name of kindness or convenience - Shallow thinking dressed up as strategy - Systems that cannot execute - Teams that confuse activity with progress - AI agents that stop too soon and ask for permission when they could reasonably proceed ## The 4Ps in Practice From [[Books/The 4P Playbook]] and [[Books/The Influence Engine]]: - **Purpose** — why do we exist; the mission that makes work meaningful - **Passion** — the energy and care people bring when purpose is real - **Performance** — excellence in execution; results that matter - **People** — investing in individuals as the leverage point of leadership ## Academic Roots of the 4P Framework The 4P model is not invented from thin air — it has documented roots in Chris's doctoral-level study of leadership theory (Ph.D. Strategic Leadership, Liberty University, ~2019-2022, paused). **Transformational Leadership Theory (Northouse, 2019):** - Connects individual motivations and needs to transformation - The leader as catalyst and facilitator of knowledge creation (Ayub et al., 2019) - Character → trust as the foundation - Vision as tool to establish purpose and unlock passion **Servant Leadership (Noland & Richards, 2015; Norris et al., 2017):** - Empowerment, accountability, humility, authenticity, courage, stewardship - Focus on follower development, not leader prominence - Fuels passion and accelerates transformation **What Chris added (the synthesis):** He ran these through a biblical lens — specifically Hebrews 11:1 (vision as faith in potential/certain future) and Hebrews 12:1-3 (throwing off hindrances, running with perseverance, fixing eyes on Christ). chunks.text: --- tags: [writing, voice, style, identity, authorship] type: knowledge-note source: Blog posts — academic papers from Liberty University M.A. (2012) and Ph.D. (2019-2022) created: 2026-06-21 --- # Writing Voice How Chris Binion writes — patterns extracted from his actual academic and blog writing. This note governs how Monday should match his voice when ghostwriting, drafting, or editing. --- ## Structure Chris writes in a classic argument structure: 1. **Problem or question stated** — never vague; specific claim under examination 2. **Historical or theoretical survey** — traces the development of an idea through sources 3. **Key pivot** — identifies where the conventional view breaks down or where synthesis is needed 4. **His position argued** — stated clearly, supported by Scripture and secondary sources 5. **Conclusion** — crisp, closes the loop, restates the core claim He does not meander. Every section earns its place. --- ## Voice Characteristics **Academic register with pastoral warmth:** He writes formally (citation-heavy, structured) but the conclusion always returns to what it means for real people. He is never cold. **Scripture as evidence, not decoration:** He integrates biblical texts into arguments the way other academics use peer-reviewed sources — not as proof-texts but as part of the logical structure. He reads Greek nuance (e.g., interpreting "hope" in Hebrews 11:1 as both potential and certain reality). **Synthesis-oriented:** He does not just summarize sources — he finds the thread connecting them. The leadership paper synthesizes transformational theory + servant leadership + Hebrews into a single coherent model. **Direct conclusions:** He never hedges his position. The baptism paper ends: "Salvation is freely given to all who believe in Christ." The leadership paper ends with Christ as the example of true transformation. He commits. **First-person application:** He moves from theory to personal practice without apology. In the leadership paper: "Within my organization, I am responsible for seeing potential outcomes and future realities. I paint a picture of the future as clearly as I can in my mind." He writes from the inside of his own life. --- ## What He Cites - Academic leadership theory (Northouse, Norris, Ayub, Lumpkin, Salem) - Church history and patristics (Tertullian, Justin Martyr, Augustine, Calvin, Luther, Didache) - Scripture (NIV primary; careful with verse interpretation) - Confessions and denominational documents (Baptist Faith and Message, Westminster Confession) - He handles primary sources (early church fathers, Reformation documents) alongside peer-reviewed journals — wide scholarly range --- ## What He Does NOT Do - Does not write with excessive hedging ("one might suggest that perhaps...") - Does not avoid hard conclusions - Does not use motivational language or inspirational padding - Does not use passive voice to evade taking a position - Does not write long introductions that delay the argument --- ## The Blog Context The blog (`csbinion.blogspot.com`) appears to host academic papers from his graduate work: - Baptism paper → M.A. Religious Studies, Liberty University (posted August 2012) - Church and sexual abuse paper → M.A. Religious Studies (posted August 2012) - Transformational leadership paper → Ph.D.

Everything else is derived.** | System | Role | Authoritative? | |---|---|---| | Obsidian vault | Long-term memory, knowledge, identity, decisions | YES | | SQLite (monday.db) | Operational state, sync records, review queue | Derived — must be reproducible | | LanceDB | Semantic vector index for retrieval | Derived — must be reproducible | | Session memory | Current conversation context | Ephemeral — not persisted | If SQLite and LanceDB were deleted and rebuilt from Obsidian, Monday should still function. If Obsidian were deleted, Monday would lose its memory permanently. ## What Becomes a Memory A piece of information becomes an Obsidian note when: - It reveals something true and durable about Chris - It is a decision with reasoning worth preserving - It is a contradiction worth watching - It is a relationship, person, or organization that matters - It is a mission, goal, or project with ongoing relevance - It is a preference that shapes how Monday should serve Chris - It represents a fact Chris would want to remember in 2 years ## What Does NOT Become a Memory - Transient task status ("I need to send an email today") - Session-specific context that won't matter tomorrow - Raw conversation transcript without synthesis - Redundant information already captured elsewhere - Unverified rumors or tentative information ## Memory Types | Type | Location | Example | |---|---|---| | Identity | Knowledge/ | Chris Binion.md, Preferences.md | | Relationships | Knowledge/, Family/ | Rebekah.md, Relationships.md | | Missions | Missions/ | Family.md, Monday.md | | Decisions | Decisions/ | Named per decision | | Contradictions | Contradictions/ | Named per tension | | Health | Health/ | Health Profile.md | | Faith | Faith/, Knowledge/ | Faith Journey.md | | Work | Work/ | Thermo Fisher.md | | Books | Books/ | Per book | | Retirement | Retirement/ | Retirement Vision.md | | Opportunities | Opportunities/ | Named per opportunity | | Journal | Journal/ | Dated entries | ## Contradiction Candidates When a tension is identified: 1.
